title: Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (Executive Order)
date_evidence: <meta property="article:published_time" content="2025-12-11T23:58:32+00:00"> ... visible dateline: Executive Orders December 11, 2025
key_claim: The 11 December 2025 executive order does not itself preempt state law; it directs the DOJ to establish an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws, directs Commerce to publish an evaluation of 'onerous' state AI laws and to make states with such laws ineligible for remaining BEAD broadband funds, directs agencies to consider conditioning discretionary grants on states not enforcing disfavored AI laws, directs the FTC and FCC to act, and calls for a legislative recommendation; a uniform national standard preempting state law would require Congress.
notes: Tier 1 primary instrument. Structural anchor (3-6m band): the canonical document establishing the coordination/funding/litigation mechanisms that constitute 'managed federalism'. Cited inline like any other source.

title: President Donald J. Trump Unveils National AI Legislative Framework
date_evidence: President Donald J. Trump Unveils National AI Legislative Framework. The White House. March 20, 2026
key_claim: The 20 March 2026 National AI Legislative Framework sets out six legislative objectives and states the framework 'can succeed only if it is applied uniformly across the United States' because 'a patchwork of conflicting state laws would undermine American innovation'; it is a set of recommendations to Congress, not binding law, and the administration 'looks forward to working with Congress in the coming months to turn this framework into legislation that the President can sign.'
verbatim_quote: a patchwork of conflicting state laws would undermine American innovation
notes: Tier 1 primary government source. The recalibrated framework; basis for the counter-argument that Congress could still legislate a real national standard.

title: Justice Department Intervenes in xAI lawsuit Challenging Colorado's 'Algorithmic Discrimination' Law
date_evidence: Press Release. Justice Department Intervenes in xAI lawsuit Challenging Colorado's 'Algorithmic Discrimination' Law. Friday, April 24, 2026
key_claim: On 24 April 2026 the DOJ moved to intervene in xAI's lawsuit challenging Colorado's AI Act (SB24-205) - the first time the federal government has moved to invalidate a state AI law - alleging the law violates the Equal Protection Clause; xAI filed the underlying suit on 9 April; the statute requires AI developers and deployers to meet disclosure, reporting and prevention requirements for high-risk uses such as mortgage lending, admissions and hiring.
notes: Tier 1 primary government source. First operational use of the EO's litigation track.

title: States can - and should - regulate AI in criminal justice
date_evidence: Chiraag Bains, Alex Chohlas-Wood, Katie Kinsey. April 16, 2026
key_claim: An executive order has no preemptive power; it is not a law and the president cannot unilaterally override state statutes; the December 2025 order merely directs agencies toward pathways that 'might eventually create pathways for preemption - and each pathway faces serious legal obstacles'; the order is 'designed to intimidate' through DOJ litigation, funding threats and FTC/FCC action; the March 2026 framework is 'a vague and abstract roadmap' rather than enforceable standards.
verbatim_quote: The order itself has no preemptive power whatsoever.
notes: Tier 2 think-tank analysis. Establishes that the EO lacks legal preemptive force and operates as intimidation/leverage - the core of the signal.

title: Regulatory Fragmentation: From Anomaly to Strategic Focus
key_claim: Regulatory fragmentation across federal, state and global jurisdictions has shifted from exception to a defining feature of the business environment, directly affecting where companies grow and how they structure products, data and governance; AI rules are fragmenting across the EU AI Act and US state AI and automated-decision laws, forcing companies to run multiple risk classifications, documentation standards and model-governance processes; boards should treat fragmentation as an enterprise risk managed strategically rather than as a siloed compliance issue.
notes: Tier 2 major-consultancy board-advisory piece. Anchors the decision-relevance: fragmentation is now a strategic, enterprise-level reality for companies.

title: How the Executive Branch Is Reshaping AI Federalism
key_claim: The December 2025 order did not formally preempt state law; it deploys executive coordination, conditional funding and litigation to sidestep the preemption question - a model the authors term 'managed federalism' in which state authority is preserved in theory but constrained in practice; state AI bills in Utah, Missouri and Louisiana have stalled or been narrowed after federal pressure and funding threats; the effect is 'attenuation' of state lawmaking, achieved before the fact rather than by contesting laws afterward, and the toolkit is transferable beyond AI.
notes: Tier 3 specialist legal analysis (Jim W. Ko and Jonathan Stroud). Source of the 'managed federalism' framing and the state-bill-stalling evidence.

title: The Colorado AI Act Hits a Wall - Litigation, Legislative Uncertainty, and an Enforcement Standstill
date_evidence: by: Kyle R. Fath, Squire Patton Boggs (US) LLP. Friday, May 1, 2026
key_claim: Colorado's AI Act (SB24-205) is effectively frozen weeks before its 30 June 2026 effective date: a magistrate judge stayed enforcement on 27 April 2026 after xAI sued on 9 April and the DOJ intervened; the Colorado Attorney General has committed not to promulgate implementing rules or enforce the Act until the legislative session concludes and rulemaking finishes; a legislative replacement narrowing the Act's scope and pushing the effective date to 1 January 2027 is under negotiation as the legislature's mid-May adjournment approaches.
notes: Tier 3 law-firm analysis published via The National Law Review. The concrete case study of managed federalism in operation.
